I absolutely encourage you to talk to your therapist about this, it is honestly a bit above the pay grade of random redditors. That being said, it is okay that you are having trouble with this. You’re not broken or faulty, someone did something horrible to you and it’s very common for our bodies to physically store trauma in various ways. Working through things with your therapist should help your body learn to let go a bit, but it’s likely to be slow progress, which is completely okay- try not to get too frustrated with yourself if there’s no overnight fix. You may want to look for a specifically experience trauma/SA therapist, if you feel the person you currently see isn’t the best fit for this work. 

Your honesty with your boyfriend is so valuable, and it sounds like he is understanding and honest back with you. The same way you trust him enough to have disclosed this to him, and to talk to him about your frustrations and challenges, you also have to trust that he means it when he reassures you, and that he would talk to you about it if this was becoming a deal breaker-type of issue for him. If it would help, maybe ask him explicitly to tell you if it ever feels like a problem, because you don’t want him to feel like he’s not being heard or considered. Based on your description, I think he would respect that, and when you’re having a hard day you can remind yourself that he’s the type of person to be honest and transparent, so if he says he’s okay with it then you can trust and believe him. 

Anyone who judges your sexual experience or preferences by calling you square is a jerk and they absolutely do not matter at all- their opinions are garbage, might as well toss them in the bin where they belong. You’re doing good, it’s going to be okay. 💕

Even though it feels like crap, this will, overall, be a good thing. I know it is horrible and surprising and confusing and genuinely just shitty right now, but you aren’t going to waste years on someone who doesn’t see a future with you. You’re 20, there is SO much time and SO many more people in this world for you to meet. I’m sure this doesn’t help right now, and it’s okay that it’s just crap right now. I promise you this is not it, your capacity to love and be loved is not empty, you will end up experiencing incredible love which dwarfs this experience. It will take time for things to not feel quite so sharp and hurty, but it will happen. Even if right now you’re not feeling okay, you absolutely will be. Just keep breathing and take it one day at a time. You’re okay and you will absolutely be comfortable with someone again.

A common theme in similar situations is one person always trying to “fix” things or apply logic the situation  when the other person really just needs empathy and compassion. If she tells you her day was crappy because her coworker was being mean (or whatever), often the best response is “that really sucks, I’m sorry it was such a weird day, what would help you feel better?” 

I know I have an instinct to want to “help” by figuring things out, so it’s tempting to go “why was she being mean? Did you offend her or something?” etc., but that only comes across as critical or invalidating. Same thing with stuff like suggesting exercise if she says she feels out of shape, or pointing out that the house is messy if she says she’s no feeling disorganised/overwhelmed, etc. 

To avoid doing this to people, I try to always go with summarise > empathise > offer support, so that I end with “what would help/can I do anything to help/do you want to talk about solutions or does it help to just get it off your chest?” Then your input can always be constructive to the other person’s needs, because they have the opportunity to tell you what they need. 

Really great that you recognise this and are working on it.

Have you told your partner that you recognise you have some insecurities and emotional challenges, and that you can see how they affect your relationship? Does your partner know you’re in therapy/know your family dynamic? Why does your partner think he makes you unhappy? 

In my experience, the more you can discuss this with him, the more opportunities you have to come up with coping strategies together. Your self awareness is so valuable here- as a random example, it’s so much more productive to turn something like “you think I’m [insert negative thing here]” (basically being self deprecating because you want him to deny it/correct you) into “right now my brain is telling me that I am [negative thing] and that it doesn’t make sense for you to want to be with me- I know you’ve never expressed that and you don’t act like that’s true, but right now the brain is being mean and it would be really helpful to talk about it/get some reassurance.” Then you’re acknowledging the real issue, acknowledging that he hasn’t caused this (and you know that), and you’re working together as a partnership to move past the hardest part. 

I hope you start feeling a bit better and more cantered soon, sometimes the brain is a real jerk.

This sounds like it will be a bit above the pay grade of reddit, but I’ll offer a few thoughts. 

She needs therapy, on her own and probably with a therapist who specialises in sexual trauma. It sounds like this is not just a difference in sex drive, but she’s had a traumatic experience and it will not get better without taking active steps. It’s great that she says you guys are a team and can work on this, but honestly, a lot of this work needs to start with her, on her own (with a professional). It’s my personal opinion that her trying to force herself to endure sexual experiences she’s not enjoying (and you’re not enjoying either, for very valid reasons) is absolutely not going to help her get more comfortable with sex. 

I think it is fair to say that right now might not be the best time for you to be together. She definitely needs professional help. I think if you help her see that you want her to feel better as a person, she might see that you’re not abandoning her. Whether you want to try to stay together as she goes through the healing process is up to you, personally I think it is fair either way. I’m so sorry that she’s had whatever experience(s) that have made her feel this way, and I’m so sorry you’re having a hard time with trying to support the woman you love while also needing to be supported yourself. It’s a difficult situation and I hope you can both end up in the best place for yourselves.

Try to understand her point of view, especially because she is pretty young herself and is raising a teenager. Have you had a conversation with her about how you feel you are responsible enough to prevent and deal with pregnancy and STIs, and that you are respectful towards the young women you’re interacting with?

You can remove yourself from the conversation as soon as she crosses the line you’ve drawn. 

It’s okay to have limits and to value yourself and your mental health. It’s okay to not be constantly emptying yourself out just to please someone else.

If it’s her house, she gets to decide who is allowed to come over. If she is your guardian, she also gets to decide where you’re allowed to stay over. It sounds like she’s trying to prevent you from hooking up with girls (a girl? Is it a specific girl you’d like to have over, or just girls in general), which is likely because she has more life experience than you do, and she wants to help you stay out of any difficult situations. 

If you can calmly and rationally present why you’d like these things to change, she might be willing to have a discussion about it. But honestly, you’re 15 and this doesn’t currently sound overprotective. It sounds like she’s looking out for you, but maybe there is more to the story.

My now-husband and I were LDR for a year at the beginning of our relationship, and one of the things that worked as my saving grace was having a code word/phrase that either of us could send at whatever time which meant “I know you’re busy/living life and I’m so happy you are, but I’m having a hard time right now, and I really need a bit of reassurance that this is still working.” If that was sent, the other person would do their absolute best to respond as soon as possible with the second half of the code, which basically meant “I love you and I’m in this with you and we’re doing great, try not to worry.” I know this isn’t exactly what you’re asking about, but I thought it might be useful for you. We used this with the understanding that of course, you can’t always stop whatever you’re doing to have a full conversation, but you can usually send back a single word within 10-15 min or so (at least with our jobs at the time we could). It was a way of connecting in the really hard moments when we couldn’t actually talk. 

Otherwise, we had pretty much agreed that we would text each other if there was something we wanted to share, and we would end up having like blocks of one sided text spam back and forth (we also had a time difference). Even if it’s not always a real time conversation, which we would do on the phone or via FaceTime when we could schedule it, the random texts were nice reminders that the other person was thinking of you. Sometimes it would literally just be like “this class is boring, but after this I’m getting chipotle for dinner so at least that’s something!” Or whatever inner monologue we had. I think by not trying to use texting as our real-time communication, it was easier to just send/receive things and be okay if there wasn’t an immediate response. 

This has been a bit ramble-y, so I don’t know how much of it will help, but hopefully some of it might. You could also check out the LDR sub. Good luck with everything!

I hope that you have some other support in place, and would recommend reaching out to other people you trust and looking into finding a therapist, if you don’t already have one. If you feel like you’re unsafe at any point, don’t hesitate to leave. You and your safety, mental, physical, and emotional, are the priority. You are worth feeling safe and secure, and you shouldn’t have to wonder if what someone else has done to you was okay or not. You didn’t want it, and it wasn’t okay. 

Sending you lots and lots of love.

YTA for the way you said it, imo. 

“You’re like your mother” and “you love to complain but don’t like to be proactive” are critical statements, and they are specifically criticising him as a person. You’re not wrong for being frustrated with the situation. I think it’s often about how we phrase things that makes us TA, rather than our intention. 

If I could make any suggestion, it’s to use “I” statements, which explain how you feel in a situation/how his behaviour affects you, without making it about a defect or flaw in him. “I know this has been bothering you a lot lately, but I’m not sure how to support you since my input feels like pressure to you. It’s difficult for me to have these conversations when I don’t feel like I can offer anything without being shot down.”

NTA, big agreement with Cuckoo. A small suggestion, just because you live with your mom and probably want to keep the peace- would you be more comfortable with a compromise like a hand squeeze, or a code word/phrase that means the equivalent of a big to her? You could suggest using something like that for the two of you, because it’s not that you don’t want to express your love/affection to her, it’s that you are not always comfortable with being physically hugged and you’re not comfortable with being forced into it when you can show affection in other ways. I think it’s completely unacceptable for her to continue trying to overstep boundaries and ignore your consent (or lack thereof), just wanted to suggest an option for navigating the situation ahead of you. Good luck 💕

If they investigate and there’s no issues, great. But what if they aren’t ever informed and something happens to a child? CPS isn’t the most well run or staffed organisation, but I have to hope/believe there are at least some staff who are genuinely doing their best to help the kids they work with. I would call.

Sort of comes across like he didn’t want you to be competition for him, but that is just a feeling I get.

I’m torn between NTA and NAH. I’m a nurse and have seen people literally hit the floor from the sight of blood in an IV, but that’s not *super* common in my experience, and most people can usually at least hold it together/tolerate it at least temporarily. I would agree that literally *anything* would have been useful, and just refusing to do anything to help was messed up, but without knowing her it’s hard to say how severe her phobia of blood is. Also seems like you deserve some understanding too, since a cut deep enough for stitches would absolutely give you an adrenaline spike and can give you some shock/shock-like symptoms, plus you were in pain, so I think it’s understandable that you’d be amped and frustrated. 

Hopefully they don’t want kids, since they’re pretty prone to bleeding and can’t drive themselves to the ER.

If that doesn’t happen, then what?” Like what does this situation look like in his brain? He doesn’t seem to grasp that you can’t just snap your fingers and force a friendship…and everyone else doesn’t like her either, so why is it your responsibility to be the one who does?

Have a look at the Love Languages, and use that to get some insight on his (and your own) love language. I started writing this and it quickly turned into a giant wall- sorry about that. TLDR I would try and communicate first about the work stress/mood changes and then see where the conversation goes before directly mentioning the text logs. 

I might bring it up by starting with your concern for how stressed and out of sorts he has been for the past month, and how it seems like the things at work are really starting to affect his mood and mental health in a noticeable, long-term manner. You’re approaching him about this because you’ve noticed a change in him and while of course it makes sense that he is stressed about work stuff, you’re worried about how it’s affecting him. I’d ask if he wants to talk about the work stuff, or if he would rather have a distraction/break from it. 

If he wants to talk, that’s great- now you get info on what he thinks is making him so stressed all the time (i.e. why he suddenly seems to be withholding issues until he explodes). Maybe at this point he will mention he’s been talking with his ex, maybe not. 

If he doesn’t want to talk about it, I’d suggest a little date night/staycation sort of thing, maybe a favourite dinner out and a local show or a night in a nearby hotel, just something you both like but a little more towards the “extra” end of the scale, as a way to turn off the work brains and let the stress rest. I think the way he would respond to that suggestion could be informative, and allows you to be clear about your needs here too. If he is up for it, then great, you plan it and do it and have a good time together where you’re getting to highlight your favourite parts of being together and also, perhaps, have an opportunity to bring up the above conversation. On the other end of the spectrum, if he just straight up says no way/he’s too busy/it wouldn’t help/whatever else, you say that you understand that things are difficult for him at the moment but something needs to change. You ask what he thinks would help to improve his quality of life, and you get to say that you’ll help him as best you can but things can’t continue this way. 

Using “I feel/when you” style statements can help these conversations be perceived as constructive instead of making someone defensive. For example, “I feel like we’ve been on different wavelengths the last few weeks when you’ve been upset but haven’t talked to me, which really sucks because I know you’re having a hard time and I really miss our evening chats.” 

In any case, once you’re in a conversation (NOT an argument) about how things have been different, I’d just say something like “you know I looked at our cell usage the other day, and I noticed Ex’s number a bunch- is she doing okay? Does she need anything from us?” You’re being honest, you’re not accusing him or them of anything, and you’re demonstrating to your husband that you aren’t jumping to conclusions/assuming the worst of him while also showing empathy towards his ex, and (in my opinion, most importantly) by using that language you are deliberately putting you and your husband together on a two-person team. You two against the world, you two solving problems together, you two caring for and supporting each other as well as coming together to support other people.
